blocks.text: Abstract. Two-column layouts are common in papers and magazines. The extractor must read the left column completely before the right one, and it must never interleave lines that merely share a baseline.

Multi-column pages place two or more text columns side by side. Their lines are often aligned to a common baseline grid, so a naive reader that sorts glyphs by height alone produces sentences that jump across the gutter on every line.
The gutter between columns is a vertical band of white space that runs through most of the page. Finding it is the first step towards a correct reading order for the body text on the page.

Once the gutter is known, every line can be assigned to the column on its side. Lines that cross the gutter, such as a title or a wide figure caption, split the page into zones that are read from top to bottom.
Inside each zone the left column is read first and the right column second. Within a column the lines simply follow each other from top to bottom, and paragraphs are separated by indentation.

Figure 1: A wide caption that crosses the gutter splits the page into two zones of columns.
Below the figure the two columns resume. This second zone must be read after the caption and must again keep the left column before the right column.
The right column of the second zone closes the page. Its first line shares a baseline with the first line of the left column in the same zone.
